name: Theodore Abu Qurrah
otherNames: Theodor Abu Qurra, in Georg Graf's German; Graf says Abu Qurra is the right reading of the Greek form and means father of refreshment
Theodorus Abucara, the Latin form of the Greek opuscula in Jacob Gretser's edition
Theodorikus Puggala, in Michael the Syrian's Chronicle as Graf translates it; Graf reads Puggala as radish-seller, a mocking twist on his name
Theodoriqi of Harran, in Barhebraeus, as Graf reports him
Epikur, in the Armenian historian Vardan, as quoted by Erwand Ter-Minassiantz and identified by Heinrich Goussen, Graf reports
knownFor: A Chalcedonian Christian under Muslim rule, called bishop of Harran in most of his Arabic works, whom Georg Graf calls the first Christian author yet known to write in Arabic. He argued for the council of Chalcedon against the Jacobites and defended the honoring of images.
dates: Georg Graf places his life roughly between 740 and 820. Paul Peeters, writing in 1917 to 1919, has him born about the middle of the eighth century and dead, it seems, before 820 (the scan reads 520). J. A. Fabricius and Andrea Gallandi have him flourish about 770, and Migne's edition carries the running date 770. Graf dates the letter to the Armenians to 811 to 813, and argues that part of his writing came before 787. Michael the Syrian dates the Armenian debate to the Greek year 1125, which Graf reckons as 813. No source gives a date for his birth, his consecration or his death
place: Edessa, where Graf places his birth; Mar Saba near Jerusalem, where Graf holds he lived; Harran in Mesopotamia, his see by most of his Arabic works; Jerusalem, where he met David at the holy places; Armenia, at the court of the prince Ashot, by Graf's reading of Abu Ra'ita and Michael the Syrian
role: Bishop of Harran, by the headings of his Arabic works; theologian and debater who wrote in Arabic

keyWorks.title: Letter to David the Jacobite
keyWorks.about: Graf's Treatise X. An answer to David, whom Theodore met when both came to pray at the holy places in Jerusalem. David asked how Christ can be two natures without being two persons, and wanted the answer by dialectic and analogy. The heading says David became orthodox. Held in Graf's German

keyWorks.title: Treatise on the honoring of images
keyWorks.about: Graf's Treatise XI, written for Janah, whom Graf takes to be a bishop. Christians were giving up the honoring of images, Theodore says, because those who claim a book revealed by God mocked them as idol-worshippers. Graf notes how carefully it treats its Muslim critics, beside harsh words for the Jews. Graf says it came from a Mar Saba manuscript written in 877, now in the British Museum. Held in Graf's German

keyWorks.title: Letter of Thomas of Jerusalem to the Armenians
keyWorks.about: Greek opusculum IV. Its heading says Theodore dictated it in Arabic for Thomas, patriarch of Jerusalem, and Michael the Syncellus, the patriarch's secretary, put it into Greek and carried it. Graf dates it to 811 to 813. Held in Gretser's Greek and Latin, reprinted by Migne

traces: The copies of all his Arabic works trace back to Mar Saba, Graf says, among them a British Museum manuscript of 877 and a copy made in 1735 by Basilius Finan from an exemplar dated 1051.
Jacob Gretser, a Jesuit of Ingolstadt, first printed 42 Greek opuscula under his name in 1606; Gallandi counts 43.
A Georgian Life of John and Euthymius, translated by Paul Peeters, says the Athonite abbot Euthymius put Abucura from Georgian into Greek. Graf gives Euthymius's death as 1028.
Euthymius as-Saifi, Melkite archbishop of Tyre and Sidon, quoted his treatise on church authority in a circular of 1720 urging union with Rome, Graf says.
Western theologians quoted his Greek works: Hugo Grotius in 1617, and Denis Petavius, whom John Henry Newman cites in his notes to Athanasius.
remembered: Graf says only his fame as a skilled debater lived on, even among hostile historians, and that his works did not live on in their homeland. Graf found no later Christian Arabic writer who cites him before 1720.
A Georgian history of Mar Saba, which Graf cites from Heinrich Goussen, calls him the youngest fruit of blessed Saba, the chief shepherd of Syria and the wonder-worker of Babylonia.
Barhebraeus, as Graf reports him, sets Theodoriqi of Harran beside Maximus and John of Damascus.
Gretser called him learned, sharp, elegant, and an unbeaten tamer of monsters.

uncertain: Most of what is known of his life is Georg Graf's reconstruction of 1910. His birth at Edessa and his stay at Mar Saba are Graf's inferences, and his life of roughly 740 to 820 is Graf's estimate. Michael the Syrian's account is known here only through Graf's German translation; Michael's own text of it is not among the sources.

His see. Most of the Arabic headings say Harran, and Graf follows them, as did Turrianus, Cotelier and Ittig. The Greek headings say Karai. The notice from Angelo Mai's library reports a Vatican manuscript that reads Charran. Michel Le Quien placed the see at Cara beyond the Jordan; Fabricius would not agree, and Gallandi says Fabricius did not rate the argument. Gretser and J. S. Assemani took it for Caria in Asia Minor.

Theodore of Caria. Gretser took him for Theodore, bishop of Caria, who sided with Photius and then sought pardon at the council of 869. Gretser saw that Theodore would then have studied with John of Damascus as a boy, or been past eighty in 869. Assemani followed him. Fabricius, Le Quien and the Mai notice keep the two men apart. Graf says the identification rests only on the puzzling word Photius in the heading of one short opusculum.

Pupil of John of Damascus. Turrianus, who translated some of the opuscula, Fabricius, Le Quien and Gallandi say so, from a Greek dialogue whose heading says it was taken down from John's voice. Graf says that heading counts for little until the dialogue is shown to be genuine, and finds no direct proof. John died before 754, Graf says, and on 4 December 749 by Siméon Vailhé; Fabricius has him die about 756. Graf allows John's personal or at least literary influence.
Edessa. Graf reads Theodore's words about Edessa, our city, as naming his home town. Michael the Syrian also calls him a man from Edessa.

Mar Saba. Graf takes the stay as settled because all the copies trace back there. He doubts a mention of Saint Sabas at the close of the letter to David, since a copyist's note follows it. A Georgian history of Mar Saba names him among its sons, through Goussen.

Abu Ra'ita of Takrit, a Jacobite contemporary who wrote against him, is known only through Graf's German, from a Paris manuscript written in 1654. Abu Ra'ita calls him the wise man, the philosopher and the scholar, and charges him with hidden Nestorian views and with insulting the Jacobite form of the Thrice-Holy hymn. The patrician of the third letter is named in the fourth. Graf identifies him as Ashot, son of Sembat, an Armenian prince of the Bagratid house, whom Graf dates 804 to 824 from Samuel of Ani.

Michael the Syrian, a Jacobite chronicler who died in 1199, says Theodorikus Puggala was briefly bishop of Harran and was disciplined by his patriarch Theodoret. He says he went to Alexandria, then to the patrician Ashot in Armenia, where Nonnus of Nisibis, sent by the Jacobite patriarch Cyriacus, beat him in debate. Graf calls Michael partisan. He accepts the points other witnesses confirm, such as Edessa, Harran and the dealings with Ashot, and rejects the deposition, the journey to Alexandria and the defeat as one-sided.

An Armenian account, from Vardan as quoted by Erwand Ter-Minassiantz, has the Syrian deacon Nana defeat a Chalcedonian named Epikur, who wanted the prince Ashot Bagratuni to accept Chalcedon. Goussen identifies Epikur with Theodore and Nana with Nonnus, Graf reports.

The letter to the Armenians. Graf dates it to 811 to 813, the years Michael the Syncellus served Thomas. Graf gives Thomas's patriarchate as about 807 to 821. A note by Harles in Migne's edition says Thomas held it not before 802; the Mai notice puts him soon after the council of 787. Graf renders the heading as calling Theodore one who was bishop of Karai.

Writing before 787. Graf argues from silence. Theodore cites the first six councils and never the seventh, of 787, which approved the honoring of images, even in his treatise on images. Graf also says that treatise allows an even less exact dating than the letter to David.

The debates before the caliph al-Ma'mun. Several manuscripts carry them, and Eusèbe Renaudot, in 1713, lists one as his. Graf rejects them as his work and denies that they took place. Whether Theodore ever argued with the caliph, Graf says, can be neither proved nor ruled out.
That David became orthodox is the claim of the letter's heading. Graf dates the letter only loosely, to the reigns of the caliphs Harun al-Rashid and al-Ma'mun.
